title: Benchmark report read-through v1 (claims + charts + methodology wording)
summary: Internal read-through of the benchmark report draft (v1). Team aligned on where language is too absolute ("best", "wins", "proves") and needs softening with variance/confidence language and scope constraints. Reviewed chart semantics (axes, units, and what latency/$ actually represents), and agreed to tighten methodology wording around warmup, caching policy, pricing assumptions, and regional comparability. Legal flagged a few external-claim risks and asked for explicit disclaimers + a review checklist before publication. Docs/web team noted landing page FAQ must mirror report wording to avoid support escalations.
topics:
1) Executive summary claims
2) Definition of latency/$ and how we compute it
3) Variance / confidence language + rerun policy references
4) Chart review: region split, model families, p50 vs p95
5) Methodology appendix wording: warmup, caching, batching, pricing assumptions
6) Disclaimers: workload representativeness, region availability, reproducibility
7) CTA and positioning alignment for Sales/SE and Support
questions: Open questions to resolve: (a) Do we say p95 anywhere in the headline callouts or keep it in appendix only? (b) Are we comfortable showing absolute $/1M tokens or only derived latency/$ index? (c) How do we phrase "Redwood regions" vs cloud-provider region names without implying equivalence? (d) Do we include a small note on routing/fallback and how it can affect customer-observed latency?

next_steps: Ethan to circulate v1.1 with revised language + inserted disclaimers
Perf/Evals to re-check any headline callouts against QC notes before finalizing charts

transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Benchmark report read-through v1 (claims + charts + methodology wording)
Date/Time: Feb 10, 2025 5:05 PM PT
Duration: 53 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees:
- Ethan Wallace (Redwood Inference)
- Camila Reyes (Redwood Inference)
- Soojin Lee (Redwood Inference)
- Jonas Weber (Redwood Inference)
- Claire Dubois (Redwood Inference)
- Sana Farid (Redwood Inference)
- Nadia Rahman (Redwood Inference)
- Wei Chen (Redwood Inference)
- Tessa Morgan (Redwood Inference)
- Laura Bennett (Redwood Inference)
- Michael Grant (Redwood Inference)
- Ben Carter (Redwood Inference)
- Elliot Price (Redwood Inference)
- Rina Kobayashi (Redwood Inference)
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference)

---
Auto-Summary (draft):
- The group agreed to soften comparative claims and add explicit scope/variance language.
- Clarified that latency/$ is a derived metric and must state exactly what latency and cost inputs are.
- Charts need consistent units (ms, tok/s, $/1M tok) and footnotes describing measurement windows.
- Landing page FAQ must match report wording to reduce support load and avoid over-claiming.

Auto-Topics:
- Executive summary language
- Chart footnotes and axes
- Methodology appendix clarity
- Legal/compliance disclaimers
- Reproducibility section

Auto-Action Items (raw):
- Revise Exec Summary.
- Add disclaimers.
- Validate cost assumptions.
- Align landing page FAQ.

---

[00:00] Ethan Wallace: Alright, I think we’re all on. Uh, goal today is a straight read-through of the report copy v1. Call out anything that feels like… over-claiming, unclear methodology, or charts that could be misread. We’ll leave with a list of edits for v1.1.

[00:27] Camila Reyes: And just to set tone: we want this to feel credible to engineers and also not get us into a “fastest on earth” thing. It’s production economics, not chest-beating.

[00:38] Soojin Lee: Yep. Also we need the landing page and the PDF to say the same thing. If the hero says “best latency per dollar” and the PDF says “in our measurements,” Support is going to get cooked.

[00:51] Ethan Wallace: Cool. I’m going to start reading Exec Summary. Stop me anytime.

[01:02] Ethan Wallace (reading): “Redwood Inference delivers the best latency per dollar across leading open models in every region we tested…”

[01:13] Michael Grant: Pause. “Best” plus “every region” plus “leading” is a three-alarm fire.

[01:18] Camila Reyes: Yeah, we can’t say “best.” We can say “measured” or “observed,” and maybe “among the configurations tested.”

[01:25] Sana Farid: Also “every region” implies zero variance and no ties. We should not be categorical.

[01:31] Ethan Wallace: Got it. So we change to something like: “In our benchmark suite across X models and Y regions, Redwood showed strong latency/$…”

[01:41] Soojin Lee: “Strong” is good. Or “competitive.” We can still have a punchy headline but it needs a qualifier.

[01:49] Markus Klein: From field perspective: if we say “best,” prospects will ask “best compared to whom” and we’ll have to dance. Better to keep it anchored: “optimized runtime + routing + batching yields lower cost for a given latency SLO.”

[02:02] Ethan Wallace: Noted.

[02:06] Ethan Wallace (reading): “Latency per dollar directly measures how quickly you can generate tokens for a fixed budget.”

[02:14] Jonas Weber: That’s directionally right but it’s ambiguous. Is it p50 latency? p95? End-to-end including network? Also “generate tokens” could be interpreted as throughput.

[02:26] Claire Dubois: Yeah. We need to say “time-to-first-token” and “time-per-output-token” are different. Our “latency” in the core table is end-to-end request latency, right? With streaming? We’re using… for chat we measured end-to-end completion with streaming enabled but we report time-to-first-token separately in internal tables.

[02:44] Ethan Wallace: In the public report we only show p50 end-to-end completion for the standard chat workload, plus p95 in appendix. That’s what we planned.

[02:54] Sana Farid: Then the definition must name it. Otherwise people assume p95.

[03:00] Nadia Rahman: And the “dollar” side — are we using list price per 1M tokens from our hosted pricing? Or measured GPU cost? Because those are different.

[03:09] Ethan Wallace: Right now the draft says “cost per 1M output tokens,” but it doesn’t explicitly say it’s Redwood API usage-based pricing.

[03:16] Nadia Rahman: We need to be explicit: it’s customer-facing token pricing for the specific SKU, in the region, during the measurement window. And note it can change.

[03:26] Michael Grant: Also: no implication that competitors use the same pricing model unless we cite them. If we aren’t benchmarking competitors directly, we should avoid drifting into comparative territory.

[03:37] Camila Reyes: Exactly. This report is “internal runs, published methodology,” not a bake-off blog.

[03:45] Ben Carter: Just to confirm, we’re not naming competitors in tables. We are only showing Redwood results by model and region.

[03:50] Ethan Wallace: Correct. But we do say “compared to building it yourself,” and we reference “managed endpoints” generally.

[03:57] Michael Grant: That’s okay if it’s clearly qualitative and not performance claims.

[04:03] Ethan Wallace: Alright. Moving on. Section 1: “Why latency per dollar.”

[04:12] Ethan Wallace (reading): “Latency/$ is the most practical metric for production because it captures user experience and unit economics.”

[04:21] Laura Bennett: I like it, but “most practical” is absolute-ish. Maybe “a practical metric” or “a useful composite metric.”

[04:29] Soojin Lee: Agree. And add one sentence: “You still need to consider quality, reliability, and tail latency.” That’s a credibility builder.

[04:37] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[04:40] Ethan Wallace: Jumping to the first chart callout. Tessa, this is the “Latency/$ by model family” bar chart.

[04:48] Tessa Morgan: Yep, chart 2. Right now the caption says “higher is better.” But I’m worried people won’t know what the units are. We used an index right now, right?

[04:58] Ethan Wallace: In this draft, yes. It’s “tokens per second per dollar” converted into an index relative to a baseline model in US-East.

[05:07] Sana Farid: If it’s indexed, the footnote must say what baseline and why. Otherwise it looks like we’re hiding absolute values.

[05:14] Ben Carter: Marketing preference was index to avoid pricing confusion and keep it visually clean. But I’m fine including a table in appendix with absolute cost per 1M tokens and p50 latency.

[05:26] Nadia Rahman: If we publish absolute cost, we have to be very sure it matches billing. I’m not opposed, but it increases risk.

[05:33] Claire Dubois: Also absolute values vary by workload (input/output mix). Our “cost per 1M tokens” assumes the standard distribution from the methodology doc.

[05:42] Ethan Wallace: So maybe we keep the main chart indexed and add an appendix table with absolute numbers + a big “under this workload definition” label.

[05:52] Michael Grant: That’s my preference. If absolute numbers are included, disclaimers must be crisp.

[06:00] Wei Chen: For docs, we can add an FAQ: “Why index?” and “Can I reproduce?” People will ask.

[06:07] Ethan Wallace: Okay. Next: region split chart.

[06:12] Ethan Wallace (reading caption): “Consistent performance across regions.”

[06:18] Jonas Weber: “Consistent” is a bit hand-wavy. We saw some region deltas due to hardware pools and network.

[06:24] Claire Dubois: Yeah, EU-West had slightly different tail behavior in one run. We reran and it tightened, but still.

[06:31] Sana Farid: We can say “same methodology applied across regions” and then show the spread. Don’t claim consistency unless we define what consistent means (like within X%).

[06:41] Markus Klein: +1. Also customers may have different routing policies. They might hit a fallback model variant or a different capacity tier. That can change latency.

[06:50] Mina? (unidentified speaker): Sorry, this is Rina. The report should say “pin model version” and “region header” because otherwise reproduction attempts will be inconsistent.

[07:00] Ethan Wallace: Yep, reproduction section covers model pinning and region selection headers. Elliot, we’ll cross-check with docs.

[07:08] Elliot Price: Yep. I saw PR about region header clarification. We should link to docs page, not put header names in the PDF, because those change.

[07:18] Ethan Wallace: Good call.

[07:22] Ethan Wallace: Methodology summary paragraph. I’ll read it.

[07:26] Ethan Wallace (reading): “We ran each model at production-level concurrency, using aggressive caching and batching to reflect real-world use.”

[07:37] Claire Dubois: “Aggressive” is risky because it sounds like we tuned for the benchmark.

[07:42] Jonas Weber: Exactly. We should say “workload-aware batching and prefix caching as supported by the platform, with fixed configuration across runs.”

[07:51] Sana Farid: And we should explicitly say the configuration is documented, and we used a consistent warmup period.

[07:59] Camila Reyes: Also there’s a narrative nuance: we do want to say “this is what customers should do in prod,” but we don’t want it to read as cherry-picked.

[08:07] Ethan Wallace: So: “We used a standardized configuration intended to reflect typical production best practices; details in appendix.”

[08:14] Michael Grant: Better.

[08:16] Nadia Rahman: One more: caching policy. We need to be precise about what was allowed. Were repeated prompts used? Did we allow prefix cache hits? If yes, that changes economics.

[08:28] Claire Dubois: In the suite, we explicitly avoided repeated prompts for the “baseline chat” workload, except for the warmup window. For the “prefix heavy” workload we did include repeated system prompts to measure prefix caching benefit.

[08:41] Ethan Wallace: The PDF right now only includes the baseline chat and embeddings. It doesn’t include prefix-heavy.

[08:48] Jonas Weber: Then don’t mention “aggressive caching” in the top-level methodology. Mention it as a platform feature later.

[08:56] Ethan Wallace: Got it. Removing.

[09:00] Ben Carter: For landing page: we still want to talk about caching/batching because it’s a key differentiator. But we can say “Redwood supports…” rather than “we used…”.

[09:10] Soojin Lee: Yes. Feature vs benchmark config.

[09:14] Ethan Wallace: Jumping to “Findings” section. First bullet: “Across tested models, Redwood delivered up to 2.1x better latency/$ than default open-source serving.”

[09:26] Michael Grant: Stop. That’s comparative.

[09:29] Camila Reyes: We don’t have the OSS baseline in the published tables, right?

[09:33] Claire Dubois: We did run a vLLM baseline internally for sanity, but we’re not publishing it.

[09:38] Sana Farid: Then we cannot publish “2.1x better” without publishing what it’s compared to and without error bars.

[09:45] Markus Klein: Also “default open-source serving” is vague. People will interpret it as vLLM on A100 with whatever flags.

[09:54] Ethan Wallace: Agree. We’ll remove that bullet entirely from public report and keep it for internal enablement maybe.

[10:02] Ben Carter: Could we rephrase as: “Redwood runtime optimizations (continuous batching, KV cache mgmt) can materially improve latency/$ compared to naïve deployments” and link to docs?

[10:12] Michael Grant: If it’s qualitative, sure. No numbers.

[10:16] Camila Reyes: And even then, keep it in blog, not in the PDF findings table.

[10:21] Ethan Wallace: Okay.

[10:25] Ethan Wallace: Next bullet: “Performance is stable across repeated runs.”

[10:31] Sana Farid: We need to define stable. In some configurations, we had 6–8% coefficient of variation on latency. That’s fine, but say “run-to-run variance was typically within X–Y% under the benchmark conditions.”

[10:44] Claire Dubois: And mention rerun rules. We had automatic reruns when variance exceeded threshold.

[10:50] Jonas Weber: We can say “multiple runs per configuration; anomalies rerun; see appendix.”

[10:56] Wei Chen: Support will ask “what if my numbers differ.” We should include a sentence: “Your observed latency may differ based on network path, prompt distribution, and routing policy.”

[11:07] Ethan Wallace: Great. That goes in FAQ too.

[11:12] Ethan Wallace: Chart 5: embeddings baseline. Caption says “Embeddings are near-linear in throughput scaling.”

[11:22] Jonas Weber: Is that actually true across all sizes? Might be too broad.

[11:26] Claire Dubois: For the specific embedding model and batch sizes we used, it was roughly linear, but I wouldn’t claim it generally.

[11:34] Sana Farid: Replace with “In our measurements, throughput scaled predictably with batch size within the tested range.”

[11:42] Ethan Wallace: Done.

[11:45] Tessa Morgan: Can we add tested batch size range in the chart footnote? Like batch=1 to 64.

[11:51] Ethan Wallace: Yes.

[11:54] Ben Carter: Also, small note: we need a “so what” for embeddings. Like “helps you estimate cost for search/retrieval.”

[12:03] Soojin Lee: Yep. And avoid “cheap.” Say “lower unit cost” or “more efficient.”

[12:10] Ethan Wallace: Alright.

[12:12] Ethan Wallace: Methodology appendix. I’ll skim what’s currently written. “We used a 10-minute warmup to populate caches.”

[12:21] Jonas Weber: That line could be misread. We didn’t “populate caches” for the measured window. Warmup is for system stability, JIT, kernel selection, etc.

[12:30] Claire Dubois: Exactly. We should say: “Warmup requests were excluded from measurement; purpose is to stabilize runtime and remove cold-start effects.”

[12:41] Ethan Wallace: Good. I’ll adjust.

[12:44] Nadia Rahman: Also, if we say “populate caches” people think we measured cache hits. We didn’t.

[12:50] Ethan Wallace: Yep.

[12:53] Michael Grant: This is important legally too. If someone interprets it as “we warmed it to look better,” that’s reputational risk.

[13:02] Camila Reyes: Right.

[13:05] Ethan Wallace: Next appendix line: “We disabled rate limiting to ensure maximum throughput.”

[13:13] Peter? (unidentified speaker): That’s not right. We didn’t disable global safety. We used a dedicated capacity window, and we rate-limited at the harness level to avoid production SLO impact.

[13:23] Ethan Wallace: Sorry—good catch. That sentence is outdated from an early harness note.

[13:29] Elliot Price: We should also be careful because rate limiting and quotas are features customers use. Saying we disabled them is weird.

[13:35] Ethan Wallace: I’ll change to: “Requests were generated by the harness with controlled concurrency; platform protections remained enabled; benchmark runs used reserved capacity windows.”

[13:48] Neha? (unidentified speaker): Sorry, this is Laura. Also mention guardrails: canary gating, rollback criteria.

[13:55] Ethan Wallace: Yep. We can add a one-liner: “Runs were executed within pre-approved capacity windows with SRE monitoring.”

[14:04] Michael Grant: That’s fine and helps credibility.

[14:08] Ethan Wallace: Next: “We compute latency per dollar as p50 latency divided by cost per token.”

[14:16] Sana Farid: That’s not exactly correct, right? Because lower is better for latency, higher is better for “per dollar.” It’s easy to invert.

[14:24] Jonas Weber: We should define it clearly and maybe give a simple example.

[14:29] Ethan Wallace: The metric in our pipeline is actually “(tokens/sec) / ($/sec)” which reduces to “tokens per dollar” but adjusted by latency under a fixed workload. Hmm.

[14:41] Claire Dubois: For the public report we should keep it simple: we report p50 latency and cost per 1M tokens separately, and latency/$ as a derived “lower latency at lower cost” composite. But if we can’t explain it in one sentence, readers will get confused.

[14:55] Ben Carter: The landing page wants a single line: “Latency per dollar: how much latency you buy with a dollar.”

[15:01] Sana Farid: That’s catchy but mathematically weird.

[15:04] Camila Reyes: We need accuracy first.

[15:07] Nadia Rahman: Suggestion: Avoid introducing a new bespoke unit. Use “cost per million tokens” and “p50 latency” prominently. Then say “latency per dollar combines these to show relative efficiency under the defined workload.”

[15:20] Michael Grant: +1. Reduce the chance of misrepresentation.

[15:24] Ethan Wallace: Okay. So the report will not overly focus on the derived metric formula. It will show both primitives and then an index.

[15:34] Markus Klein: For Sales, we can still talk about it as a simple tradeoff curve: “Here’s the frontier.” But for PDF, less formula.

[15:42] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[15:45] Ethan Wallace: Now, claims language. There’s a line: “This report proves Redwood is the most cost-effective way to serve open models.”

[15:54] Michael Grant: Delete “proves.” Replace with “illustrates” or “shows in our measurements.”

[16:00] Soojin Lee: Also “most cost-effective” is absolute. We can say “a cost-effective approach” or “can reduce unit costs.”

[16:08] Camila Reyes: And add reliability note. “Cost-effective while meeting latency targets.”

[16:14] Ethan Wallace: Okay.

[16:16] Ethan Wallace: There’s also “apples-to-apples across regions.”

[16:22] Jonas Weber: That’s dangerous. It’s never truly apples-to-apples; hardware mix can differ.

[16:28] Claire Dubois: We tried to standardize, but there are still differences. Better: “standardized methodology applied consistently across regions.”

[16:37] Sana Farid: And mention confidence intervals in a footnote. Even if we don’t show full CI bars, we can say “variance observed across repeated runs.”

[16:47] Ethan Wallace: Okay.

[16:49] Ethan Wallace: Let’s talk about chart annotations. Tessa, any other red flags?

[16:54] Tessa Morgan: Two: 1) Some charts label “APAC” as a region but don’t specify which. We should say the region name, like “Tokyo” or “Singapore,” whichever we’re using. 2) Color mapping: model families might be confusing because “Llama” and “Mistral” colors are too close.

[17:10] Ben Carter: We’re planning at least one APAC region, likely Tokyo. Use exact region label in the report.

[17:16] Elliot Price: From docs side we should call it “Redwood Region: ap-northeast-1 (Tokyo)” or whatever our canonical string is. But careful: don’t imply it’s identical to AWS region naming.

[17:27] Michael Grant: Right. Use “Redwood region (Tokyo)” and avoid referencing cloud provider regions unless we must.

[17:34] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[17:38] Ethan Wallace: Now, the section “How to interpret results.” It says: “If your app uses chat completions, you can expect similar savings.”

[17:49] Wei Chen: That will create support tickets. Needs to be: “Your results may vary; if you have different prompt lengths, different output lengths, different concurrency.”

[17:57] Markus Klein: And routing. If a customer sets aggressive latency routing, they may pay more. Or if they allow fallback to a smaller model, they may see lower cost. We should mention that policies matter.

[18:12] Claire Dubois: Also tokenization differences and sampling parameters. Temperature affects output length distribution.

[18:20] Ethan Wallace: Okay, so we make that paragraph more “here’s how to think about it” and less “you will get.”

[18:27] Sana Farid: Exactly.

[18:30] Ethan Wallace: One more line: “We measured in real production conditions.”

[18:36] Jonas Weber: That’s squishy. We measured in a controlled environment using production infrastructure, not customer traffic.

[18:44] Camila Reyes: Use “production-like conditions” or “production infrastructure with controlled load generation.”

[18:51] Michael Grant: And clarify “synthetic workload, no customer data.”

[18:56] Ethan Wallace: Got it.

[19:00] Ben Carter: Quick check: do we explicitly say “no customer prompts” in the report? That’s good for trust.

[19:06] Ethan Wallace: There’s a line in the methodology: “We used a fixed prompt set.” But we can add: “All prompts are synthetic / open prompts, not customer data.”

[19:15] Michael Grant: Yes.

[19:18] Ethan Wallace: Okay.

[19:21] Ethan Wallace: Let’s address the “Headline stats” callout box. It currently says: “Up to 40% lower latency at the same cost.”

[19:33] Sana Farid: That’s a paired comparison claim. “Same cost” compared to what? It implies a baseline.

[19:38] Claire Dubois: That came from comparing two configurations within Redwood (quant profile A vs B). Not sure it belongs.

[19:45] Camila Reyes: If it’s internal config improvement, it doesn’t help the public narrative and it can confuse.

[19:51] Ben Carter: Agree. Better headline: “Benchmarked across X models and Y regions with reproducible methodology.” Credibility first.

[20:00] Soojin Lee: We can still have an outcome-oriented line: “Optimize latency and cost without changing models.” But no numbers.

[20:08] Ethan Wallace: Okay, we’ll rewrite the callout box.

[20:12] Ethan Wallace: Next: “Model coverage.” The draft lists “Llama 3.1 70B, Mistral Large, Qwen 2.5…”

[20:22] Claire Dubois: Careful on naming; some model names might be slightly off. Also versions. If we publish a model name, it must match what’s actually in the catalog at launch.

[20:32] Elliot Price: And match docs naming.

[20:35] Jonas Weber: Also “Mistral Large” is not necessarily open weights. We should ensure we’re consistent with “open models” claim.

[20:43] Camila Reyes: Great catch. This report is “open models,” so don’t list anything that’s gated or not open weights. If we include, we need to adjust messaging.

[20:53] Ben Carter: Let’s keep it to the curated set that’s clearly open. Llama, Qwen, maybe Mixtral.

[21:00] Ethan Wallace: I’ll coordinate with Claire on the final list.

[21:04] Ethan Wallace: Now, the “methodology” bullet list includes “sequence length distribution representative of production.”

[21:13] Sana Farid: Again “representative” is tricky. Whose production? It’s our proxy.

[21:18] Jonas Weber: We can say “based on anonymized aggregate patterns we commonly observe across workloads” but even that implies we used customer data.

[21:27] Michael Grant: Avoid implying customer data unless we did a privacy review. Safer: “based on typical application patterns and internal experience.”

[21:36] Claire Dubois: We can say “short-to-medium prompts with a long-tail distribution” without claiming it’s universal.

[21:44] Ethan Wallace: Okay.

[21:46] Ethan Wallace: Reproducibility section. It says: “You can reproduce these results by running our harness.”

[21:55] Markus Klein: Customers will try and get different numbers. We should say “reproduce the methodology,” not “results.”

[22:03] Wei Chen: Yes: “reproduce the approach and compare relative changes.”

[22:09] Claire Dubois: Also we’re publishing a minimal example, not the full internal harness.

[22:15] Elliot Price: Right. Link to example repo that uses the API and outputs a smaller table.

[22:21] Ethan Wallace: Great. I’ll reword.

[22:25] Ethan Wallace: Quick legal check: we have a disclaimer paragraph at the end that starts “This report is provided as-is.” Michael, is that enough?

[22:33] Michael Grant: It’s a start, but I want more up front. A small “Methodology and limitations” callout early. And we need an approvals checklist before anything goes public.

[22:44] Camila Reyes: We have claims guidelines doc; we should align to that and make sure approvals are recorded.

[22:50] Ethan Wallace: Noted.

[22:52] Ben Carter: Also: we should avoid “guarantee” language in CTAs. The landing page currently has “Get guaranteed performance.”

[23:00] Soojin Lee: Oh, yeah, that’s not okay. We can say “SLA-backed options available” but not “guaranteed” in general.

[23:08] Markus Klein: For Dedicated, we do have SLA language, but it’s contract-specific. Better: “SLA-backed Dedicated capacity available.”

[23:16] Ethan Wallace: Okay.

[23:18] Ethan Wallace: Let’s do a quick scan of the “FAQ” in the PDF. Q: “Why not just use OpenAI?”

[23:26] Camila Reyes: That’s a blog question, not in the report PDF.

[23:29] Michael Grant: Remove it. That’s competitive and will trigger reviews.

[23:33] Ben Carter: Agreed. Competitive FAQ belongs in enablement, not public.

[23:38] Ethan Wallace: Removing.

[23:40] Ethan Wallace: Another FAQ: “Do you store prompts?”

[23:46] Wei Chen: That one is good. And we should state: benchmarks used synthetic prompts and logs are not published.

[23:53] Michael Grant: Yes, and keep it accurate to our policy. Don’t overpromise like “we never log anything.” Say “logging and retention are configurable; benchmark artifacts are internal; public tables are aggregated.”

[24:05] Nadia Rahman: Also note: cost metrics are aggregated and don’t include customer identifiers.

[24:10] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[24:13] Ethan Wallace: Charts again — there’s a y-axis labeled “Latency/$ (higher is better)” on chart 2.

[24:22] Sana Farid: That’s confusing because “latency” implies lower is better. Rename to “Efficiency index (latency/$)” or “Economics index.” Or even avoid “latency/$” on the axis and put it in the caption.

[24:34] Tessa Morgan: Yep, I can relabel as “Latency-per-dollar index” with an arrow “higher is better.” And add a tooltip for web.

[24:43] Elliot Price: For the web version, we can have hover text. For PDF, footnote.

[24:49] Ethan Wallace: Okay.

[24:52] Ethan Wallace: How do we feel about including p95 anywhere outside appendix?

[24:57] Claire Dubois: p95 is important for production, but it can complicate the narrative. If we include, we need to be consistent and explain it.

[25:05] Sana Farid: If we include p95, we must also include variability and maybe number of runs. Otherwise it’s a single p95 snapshot.

[25:12] Camila Reyes: I vote keep p95 in appendix and talk about tail latency in text.

[25:17] Markus Klein: That’s fine. In field decks we can show p95 when needed.

[25:21] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[25:24] Ben Carter: Quick note: we should add a “What’s next” section to set expectation for refresh cadence. Like “we’ll refresh quarterly.”

[25:33] Camila Reyes: Yep, but don’t promise a hard cadence if we can’t deliver.
